LLM auditresponse for .nvchecker.toml:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The file `.nvchecker.toml` is a configuration snippet for **nvchecker**, an AUR helper used to automatically fetch the latest upstream version of a project. It contains only:
- A section `[odytty]` naming the project
- `source = "github"` indicating the version‑check source
- `github = "ghreprimand/odytty"` pointing to the repository
- `use_latest_release = true` and `prefix = "v"` defining the version‑parsing rules

These lines are typical for a benign version‑check configuration. There are no network requests, command executions, obfuscation, or unexpected file operations in the file itself. The content is purely declarative and aligns with standard AUR packaging practices, posing no immediate security risk.
</details>
<evidence>
</evidence>
<summary>Simple version‑check config, no malicious behavior.</summary>
</security_assessment>

LLM auditresponse for .SRCINFO:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The `.SRCINFO` file contains only standard AUR metadata for the odytty package. It declares a source tarball from the official GitHub releases page (`https://github.com/ghreprimand/odytty/releases/download/v0.12.0/odytty-0.12.0.tar.gz`) and provides a matching SHA256 checksum. All other fields (`pkgdesc`, dependencies, architecture, etc.) follow normal packaging conventions with no inline scripts, network calls, or obfuscation. The limited architecture restriction to `x86_64` is a packaging choice, not a security issue.

Thus the file exhibits no evidence of malicious behavior and complies with typical AUR practices.
</details>
<evidence>
</evidence>
<summary>No malicious code or suspicious network activity detected.</summary>
</security_assessment>

LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This PKGBUILD follows standard Arch packaging conventions for a Rust application. The source is fetched from the project's own GitHub releases (`https://github.com/ghreprimand/odytty/releases/download/v$pkgver/odytty-$pkgver.tar.gz`), which is the expected upstream location. The `sha256sums` placeholder is a standard practice for AUR packages managed by automated tooling (as documented in the comments). The build process uses `cargo fetch --locked` and `cargo build --release --frozen`, which are the standard commands for packaging Rust projects. No suspicious commands (no `curl|bash`, `eval`, `base64`, etc.) are present. All file operations are routine package installation into `$pkgdir`. No data exfiltration, backdoors, or unexpected system modifications are detected.
</details>
<evidence>
</evidence>
<summary>Standard Rust AUR PKGBUILD with no security issues detected.</summary>
</security_assessment>

LLM auditresponse for .gitignore:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This is a standard .gitignore file for an AUR package. It uses the common pattern of ignoring all files (`*`) then explicitly allowing only the packaging-related files: `.nvchecker.toml` (for version checking), `.gitignore` itself, `PKGBUILD`, and `.SRCINFO`. This is normal AUR maintenance practice to keep the repository clean while tracking only essential build files. No malicious behavior, network requests, obfuscation, or dangerous commands are present.
</details>
<evidence>

</evidence>
<summary>
Standard AUR .gitignore file, no threats
</summary>
</security_assessment>
